checkpoints: Given slot layout of a struct, write the exact slot key and offset for each member
Explain why a contract account's nonce stays 1 while an EOA's increments per transaction
Compute max total fee for a transaction from maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas, and gas limit
Identify which operations in a trace are cold vs warm storage accesses and state the cost difference
keyConcepts: Account model: EOAs vs contract accounts, code hash, storage root, balance, nonce
Gas as metering for every EVM operation; gas limit, gas price, priority fee mechanics
Transaction fields: nonce, gasLimit, maxFeePerGas, to, value, data, signature
Storage layout: 32-byte slots, slot packing of sub-256-bit types, mapping and dynamic-array hashing schemes
Memory and calldata: volatile regions, memory expansion cost, calldata immutability
Contract ABI: function selectors (first 4 bytes of keccak256 signature), argument encoding
State trie commitments and why storage writes are the dominant cost
labs: Craft a raw transaction by hand-encoding a function selector and arguments, then broadcast it on a testnet
Deploy a contract that writes values of packed types and read the raw storage slots to verify the packing scheme
Measure gas differences between storage reads/writes, memory ops, and event emission using a local node trace
Decode the input data of five mainnet transactions with a local ABI decoder and label each call
Run a local EVM (e.g., anvil or ganache) and replay a failed out-of-gas transaction, inspecting the consumed gas breakdown
objectives: Distinguish externally owned accounts from contract accounts by code, storage, and nonce behavior
Compute the total cost of a transaction from gas price, gas used, and intrinsic cost components
Predict storage versus memory versus calldata placement for function data and its cost implications
Decode a raw transaction's input data against a contract ABI by hand
Trace how a signed transaction flows from mempool to state transition in a block
modules.title: EVM execution model

checkpoints: State exactly when fallback runs instead of receive for a payable transfer with nonempty calldata
Given two parents defining the same function, write the correct override specifier list
Explain why a mapping cannot be copied to memory and what breaks when you try
Choose the right error mechanism for: invariant violation, user input validation, and gas-optimized library code
keyConcepts: Value types: uint/int widths, address vs address payable, bytes, enums; reference types: arrays, structs, mappings
Data locations: storage, memory, calldata and the assignment rules between them
Visibility: external, public, internal, private; state mutability: pure, view, payable, nonpayable
Inheritance: linearized C3 order, virtual/override, abstract contracts and interfaces
fallback() vs receive(): when each triggers and why both should be minimal
Events: topics vs data, indexed parameter limits, LOG opcode cost
Custom errors vs require strings vs assert: failure semantics and gas refunds
Constructor semantics, immutables, and constants
labs: Write a contract with deliberate visibility mistakes, then call each function externally and internally to map the actual behavior
Build a diamond-less multi-inheritance hierarchy with conflicting overrides and verify which implementation executes
Implement a vault contract with separate receive and fallback paths; test native-token transfers, empty calldata, and unknown selectors
Replace require strings with custom errors across a contract and measure the deployment and call gas savings
Emit events with indexed and non-indexed fields, then query them with an eth_getLogs filter on a local chain
objectives: Select correct types, data locations, and visibility specifiers for a given function contract
Implement inheritance hierarchies and resolve override conflicts predictably
Design fallback and receive handlers that route native-token transfers safely
Choose between custom errors, require, and assert based on intent and gas cost
Emit indexed events that support reliable off-chain indexing of on-chain state changes
modules.title: Solidity language semantics

checkpoints: Name the three functions that make ERC-721's safeTransferFrom safe and explain the receiver check
Explain why initialize() on the proxy, not the constructor on the implementation, sets initial state
Describe a storage collision scenario between a proxy and an implementation and how to avoid it
State when to use unchecked{} and what invariant the developer must hold to use it safely
keyConcepts: ERC-20 interface: balanceOf, transfer, approve, allowance, transferFrom; allowance double-spend mitigation
ERC-721 interface: ownerOf, tokenURI, safe transfer checks against onERC721Received
Ownable: single-owner pattern, ownership transfer pitfalls; AccessControl: role identifiers, admin hierarchies
Upgradeable proxies: delegatecall-based execution, storage collision between proxy and implementation
Transparent vs UUPS proxy patterns: who holds the upgrade authorization and the upgradeTo entrypoint
Initializer pattern replacing constructors; disabling initializers on the implementation contract
Storage gaps (__gap arrays) as layout reservation for upgradeable hierarchies
SafeMath history: pre-0.8 silent wraparound, checked arithmetic defaults since 0.8.0, unchecked blocks for gas
labs: Deploy an ERC-20 with a mint role and an ERC-721 with enumerable behavior; exercise transferFrom with and without approval
Build an AccessControl system with admin, minter, and pauser roles; demonstrate a role-grant flow end to end
Deploy a UUPS proxy, upgrade its implementation to add a new function, and verify state persists across the upgrade
Write a pre-0.8-style arithmetic exploit contract in modern Solidity to show how checked math now reverts
Implement a contract with a storage gap, upgrade it with new variables, and prove no storage collision occurred
objectives: Implement an ERC-20 and ERC-721 contract using audited library primitives without hand-rolling token logic
Compare Ownable versus AccessControl and select the right pattern for role-structured systems
Deploy a UUPS or transparent proxy system and perform a live implementation upgrade
Explain the history of safe math: why explicit SafeMath was needed and what changed in Solidity 0.8
Initialize upgradeable contracts correctly, including the storage-gap discipline for future versions
modules.title: OpenZeppelin patterns: tokens, access, and upgradeability

checkpoints: Trace the exact call sequence of a reentrancy exploit against a withdraw-before-update function
Explain why tx.origin authentication fails when a user interacts through any intermediary contract
State the storage-layout precondition that makes delegatecall between two contracts safe
Identify push vs pull payment structure in a given contract and name the failure mode of the push version
keyConcepts: Reentrancy: external call before state update lets the callee re-enter; single-function vs cross-function vs cross-contract variants
Checks-effects-interactions ordering; reentrancy guards and their limits
tx.origin vs msg.sender for authentication and the phishing vector of tx.origin
delegatecall: runs callee code in caller storage context; proxy-call injection and function selector collisions
Access control failures: unprotected init functions, missing onlyOwner on sensitive setters, default visibility traps
Gas griefing: unbounded iteration over user-controlled arrays, push payments to contracts that revert
Pull-payment pattern: escrow balances and withdrawal functions as the safe payout shape
labs: Write a vulnerable withdraw function, exploit it with an attacker contract on a local chain, then fix it with checks-effects-interactions
Audit a sample contract set for missing access control and document each finding with the exact vulnerable line
Build a delegatecall proxy that gets hijacked by an attacker-supplied implementation to overwrite the owner's slot
Create a payout contract that becomes unusable when one recipient's fallback reverts, then refactor to pull payments
Write an unbounded-loop airdrop function, measure gas as the recipient list grows, and find the list size that exceeds the block limit
objectives: Explain the reentrancy attack cycle at the EVM call level and why state updates must precede external calls
Identify missing or misplaced access control by auditing modifier placement and function visibility
Detect delegatecall hazards: context preservation, storage layout alignment, and untrusted targets
Reason about gas-based denial of service: unbounded loops, push-payment patterns, and block gas limits
Apply the checks-effects-interactions pattern and pull-payment design to neutralize common control-flow bugs
modules.title: Vulnerability class deep dives I: control flow and access

checkpoints: Explain why a single-block spot price is unsafe and what TWAP changes about the attacker's cost
Describe the information an attacker needs from the mempool to sandwich a trade and the commit-reveal defense
State the rule for multiplication/division ordering to minimize precision loss and why
List the fields that must appear in an EIP-712 domain to prevent cross-chain signature replay
keyConcepts: Oracle manipulation: spot-price reads from a single DEX pool are manipulable within one block via flash capital
TWAP oracles, multi-source aggregation, staleness checks, and circuit breakers as layered defense
Front-running: public mempool ordering, sandwich attacks on DEX trades, commit-reveal as mitigation
Integer issues: truncation in division, rounding favoring one party, precision scaling with token decimals
Signature schemes: EIP-712 domain separation, nonce invalidation, malleability and replay across chains (chainId)
Timestamp dependence: miner-influenced block.timestamp and the 15-second rule of thumb for safe use
Economic DoS: forcing expensive callbacks, dusting to bloat iteration, first-depositor share inflation
labs: Build a lending contract priced by a spot DEX quote, manipulate the price in a single transaction, and drain it on a forked mainnet
Add a TWAP-based price feed and staleness check to the same contract and verify the manipulation now fails
Write a sandwich-attack simulation on a local DEX pair and measure the victim's slippage versus the attacker's profit
Implement an EIP-712 permit function, then demonstrate a cross-chain replay when chainId is omitted from the domain
Write a vault with share-price rounding that favors early depositors, then fix the rounding direction and re-verify
objectives: Model how a price oracle can be manipulated and design defenses with TWAPs and sanity bounds
Analyze front-running and MEV exposure of a transaction's public mempool visibility
Evaluate integer-related issues beyond overflow: precision loss, rounding direction, and division-before-multiplication
Assess signature replay and permit-style authorization pitfalls including nonce and domain handling
Recognize economic denial of service: dust attacks, griefing via required callbacks, and rent extraction
modules.title: Vulnerability class deep dives II: economics and ordering

checkpoints: Name three invariants for an ERC-20 vault that a fuzzer should assert after every call sequence
Explain when symbolic execution finds bugs that static detectors miss and why it scales worse
Describe what makes a fork test different from a unit test and when each is appropriate
State why branch coverage of the withdrawal path matters more than aggregate line coverage
keyConcepts: Testing layers: unit tests per function, integration tests across contracts, fork tests against mainnet state
Static analysis concepts: taint tracking, dataflow facts, known detector patterns (reentrancy, unprotected selfdestruct)
Slither-style detectors vs symbolic execution: speed and coverage tradeoffs of each approach
Fuzzing: random input generation against function selectors; stateful fuzzing with persistent chain state
Invariant testing: properties that must hold across arbitrary call sequences (e.g., sum of balances equals total supply)
Differential testing against a reference implementation for numeric correctness
Coverage pitfalls: high line coverage with zero invariant coverage gives false confidence
labs: Write a full test suite for a token vault: deposits, withdrawals, access control, and every revert branch
Run a static analyzer over the suite's contracts, then classify each finding as true positive, false positive, or informational
Build a stateful fuzz harness with the invariant that total assets always equal the sum of user shares' value
Fork mainnet state locally and test an upgrade against real token balances and allowances
Add a CI pipeline that fails on lint violations, low coverage of critical files, or new analyzer findings
objectives: Write unit tests that cover happy paths, revert paths, and access-control boundaries of a contract
Run a static analysis tool on a codebase and triage its findings into true positives and noise
Design a stateful fuzzing campaign with invariants that catch reentrancy and accounting drift
Integrate linting, formatting, and CI checks into a contract repository
Measure test coverage meaningfully: branch coverage of critical paths rather than raw line percentages
modules.title: Secure development workflow: tests, analysis, fuzzing

checkpoints: List the actors and trust boundaries in a staking contract with an admin, a keeper bot, and users
Rank three findings by severity with a one-line justification each
State the five required sections of a complete audit finding
Explain why centralization risk (admin keys) belongs in every audit report even when no code bug exists
keyConcepts: Threat modeling: enumerate assets (funds, roles, data), actors (users, admins, attackers, MEV searchers), trust boundaries
Attack surface mapping: external entrypoints, privileged functions, upgrade paths, oracle dependencies
Review order: architecture first, then access control, then arithmetic, then control flow, then economics
Finding anatomy: title, severity, description, vulnerable code location, PoC, impact, recommendation
Severity frameworks: critical/high/medium/low/informational based on impact times likelihood
Audit artifacts: scope statement, assumptions, centralization risks, acknowledged vs fixed findings
Contest and review dynamics: how time-boxed audits differ from open security contests
labs: Threat-model a two-contract staking system and list every trust boundary a privileged role crosses
Perform a timed checklist review of a provided vulnerable contract set and log each finding with severity
Write one critical finding end to end: PoC exploit contract, impact calculation in token value, and a concrete fix
Re-audit a contract after fixes are applied and classify each original finding as fixed, acknowledged, or unresolved
Draft a one-page audit scope for a DeFi protocol: in-scope files, assumptions, and excluded components
objectives: Produce a threat model for a contract system: assets, trust boundaries, actors, and attack surfaces
Conduct a checklist-driven manual review covering each vulnerability class in this sequence
Write a finding with severity, likelihood, impact, proof of concept, and remediation guidance
Prioritize findings by exploitability and economic impact rather than by code aesthetics
Scope an audit engagement: time-boxing, in-scope contracts, and out-of-scope assumptions
modules.title: Audit workflow: threat modeling to reporting

checkpoints: Explain why two identical sources can produce different deployed bytecode and what the metadata hash is
State the three roles that should never share one private key in a production deployment
Describe what a timelock guarantees users that a plain multisig does not
List the minimum items on a mainnet launch checklist before real funds are accepted
keyConcepts: Testnet staging: deploying to public testnets, faucet discipline, mirroring mainnet dependencies via forks
Source verification: flattened vs standard-json input, compiler version and optimizer settings must match exactly
Metadata hash: the appended CBOR blob and why it makes bytecode differ between identical sources
Key hygiene: hardware wallets for admin keys, never committing private keys, separating deployer from admin
Multisig and timelocks: threshold signatures for privileged actions, delay windows for user exit
Pausable patterns and emergency stops: who can pause, what pause blocks, and unpausing governance
Monitoring: event-based alerting on privileged calls, large transfers, and proxy upgrades
Launch limits: deposit caps, rate limits, and guarded launch phases for new protocols
labs: Write a deployment runbook script that deploys, initializes, verifies, and transfers ownership in one reproducible run
Verify a contract on a block explorer, then intentionally mismatch the optimizer runs and observe the verification failure
Set up a multisig wallet on a testnet, transfer contract ownership to it, and execute an admin action through the threshold
Implement a pausable token sale with a timelocked admin, then simulate an incident: pause, investigate, unpause
Build a monitoring alert on a local chain that fires when the proxy implementation address changes
objectives: Deploy a contract system through testnet staging with a documented deployment runbook
Verify contract source on a block explorer and confirm the exact deployed bytecode matches
Design a key-management plan: deployer keys, admin keys, multisig thresholds, and timelocks
Plan an incident response: pause mechanisms, upgrade paths, and communication steps for an exploit
Evaluate mainnet readiness with a launch checklist covering monitoring, limits, and rollback options
